editorNote: Lucasfilm's Games Group steps onto the home-computer stage with Ballblazer and Rescue on Fractalus!, while pens, tablets and sub-$100 word processors broaden what a family machine can do.
morningLine: From a fractal alien mountain to the printed page, this is the week home computers learned new tricks.

lead.headline: Lucasfilm Brings the Force to Home Videogames
lead.dek: The film studio unveils Ballblazer and Rescue on Fractalus!, two Atari projects built around fresh technology and a cinematic sense of play.
body: SAN RAFAEL, Calif. — Lucasfilm publicly entered the home videogame market May 8, unveiling the first two projects from a Games Group nurtured through its collaboration with Atari. The announcement puts one of cinema's most famous technical workshops behind software intended for Atari 8-bit computers and the 5200 console.

Ballblazer turns a futuristic sport into a fast split-screen contest. Each player sees the arena from a first-person viewpoint while the computer produces a changing musical accompaniment, an unusually energetic pairing of action and sound for the home screen.

The companion project, then presented as Rescue on Fractalus!, places the player in a cockpit above an alien mountain range. Its terrain draws on Loren Carpenter's fractal graphics methods, allowing the machine to suggest an expansive, jagged landscape without storing every ridge by hand.

The two games remain previews rather than finished store releases, but they signal an ambitious new studio identity. Atari supplies hardware knowledge and marketing support; Lucasfilm supplies visual research, experimentation and the expectation that a computer game can stage a world rather than merely keep score.

stories.headline: Pens and Tablets Challenge the Keyboard
body: COMPUTE!'s May cover package asks readers to imagine pointing and drawing directly at the screen. Its survey of light pens and graphics tablets presents these devices as increasingly practical alternatives to typing commands.

A companion technical article explains how the devices report position, while the issue's Digital Palette feature and a 3-D surface-plotting program turn the idea into hands-on graphics work. The $2.95 magazine captures direct manipulation moving from laboratory curiosity toward the home desk.

stories.headline: Home Word Processing Drops Below $100
body: Atari is advertising AtariWriter, a 16K-compatible ROM cartridge, at under $100. The package offers search and replace, block movement, headers and footers, form letters, print preview, automatic page numbering and even an undo command.

Professional Software answers with WordPro 3 Plus/64 and SpellRight Plus for $99.95. The competing offers show serious writing tools becoming family-budget purchases, with mail merge and spelling assistance no longer reserved for an office system.

stories.headline: Atari Searches for a New Mission
body: Creative Computing describes Atari's new watchwords as profitability, reliability and creativity after a punishing year for the videogame business. The company must restore confidence while deciding how its home computers and game machines fit together.

The report arrives before the next great corporate turn: Warner still owns the consumer operation, but pressure for a workable plan is unmistakable. Lucasfilm's imaginative previews offer one example of the distinctive software Atari needs.
